subject: PRAETOR orchestrator composition
assertion: PRAETOR's CLI (praetor.py) enumerates files once via walk_files() and dispatches to four engines (secrets, aisec, sast via Semgrep, sca via osv/pip/npm), whose findings are merged by interpret.py (dedup, then rank, then FP-filter) before report.py emits text and JSON output.

subject: static-only invariant
assertion: No PRAETOR engine executes, imports, installs, or evaluates the scanned target: secrets/aisec read files as text, Semgrep and osv-scanner are static analyzers, pip-audit runs with --disable-pip, and npm audit reads the lockfile with a pinned registry.
verbatim: No engine executes, imports, installs, or evaluates the target.

subject: PRAETOR's own network behavior
assertion: PRAETOR's own code opens no outbound sockets; only the optional SCA and Semgrep subprocesses make network calls to advisory or registry databases.
exceptions: SCA subprocesses (osv-scanner, pip-audit, npm audit) and the Semgrep registry fetch do make network calls

subject: dependency-light design principle
assertion: The orchestrator and both built-in engines (secrets, aisec) are pure Python standard library, deliberately, to keep the tool auditable and avoid a large dependency tree.

subject: graceful degradation principle
assertion: Missing external tools (Semgrep, osv-scanner) never abort a scan; the affected engine reports itself skipped and the report states that.

subject: honest triage principle
assertion: Likely false positives are surfaced with a stated reason rather than deleted, and a clean scan is reported as nothing matched, never as safe.
verbatim: A clean result is reported as "nothing matched," never "safe."

subject: walk_files directory exclusions
assertion: walk_files() skips VCS, build, and vendor noise directories but deliberately does not skip .claude/ or hooks/, because those are prime AI-security targets.
verbatim: deliberately not skipping .claude/ or hooks/ (prime AI-security targets)

subject: binary versus text file detection
assertion: Binary detection in walk_files() judges on decoded code points rather than raw bytes, so invisible-Unicode-heavy files (which aisec specifically hunts) are correctly classified as text and get scanned.

subject: Severity.parse normalizes external scales
assertion: core.py defines ordered Severity (CRITICAL..INFO) and Confidence (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW) enums, and Severity.parse normalizes external tools' severity scales (e.g. Semgrep's ERROR/WARNING/INFO, npm's moderate) into PRAETOR's own scale.
verbatim: Severity.parse normalizes external scales (Semgrep ERROR/WARNING/INFO, npm moderate, etc.)

subject: redact masks secrets in reports
assertion: core.py's redact() and redact_line() functions mask secrets so a PRAETOR report can never leak a live credential.
verbatim: mask secrets so a report can never leak a live credential

subject: secrets engine detection strategies
assertion: engine_secrets.py uses two strategies: anchored provider-pattern regexes (high confidence, filtered by a strict is_dummy placeholder check) and generic entropy-gated matches with a broad placeholder filter plus known false-positive shape exclusions, rated MEDIUM/LOW confidence by design.

subject: secrets engine base64 unwrapping
assertion: engine_secrets.py unwraps base64 blobs and re-checks the decoded content, catching base64-wrapped keys and service-account JSON; every matched secret is redacted before it leaves the engine.

subject: aisec detector families
assertion: engine_aisec.py implements five detector families mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and CWE: prompt injection, hidden content, data exfiltration, dangerous hooks (Claude Code, git, npm lifecycle scripts), and safety bypass.

subject: hidden-content Unicode Tags block severity
assertion: aisec's hidden-content detector treats the Unicode Tags block (U+E0000 to E007F, used for invisible ASCII smuggling) as CRITICAL severity, alongside zero-width and invisible Unicode, bidirectional Trojan-Source controls, and instruction-bearing HTML comments.
verbatim: the Unicode Tags block (U+E0000..E007F, invisible ASCII smuggling, CRITICAL)

subject: sast engine runtime fallback order
assertion: engine_sast.py detects a Semgrep runtime in order: native semgrep on PATH, then WSL (wsl -d <distro>), then Docker (semgrep/semgrep image with a read-only mount).

subject: sast ruleset composition
assertion: sast always runs the bundled offline baseline (rules/semgrep-praetor.yaml, which adds agent/AI-specific rules the public packs lack) and, by default, also runs Semgrep's curated registry packs (p/owasp-top-ten, p/security-audit) when the network is reachable; --no-registry disables the registry packs.
exceptions: --no-registry disables the registry packs, leaving only the bundled baseline

subject: sast reads the real source line locally
assertion: engine_sast.py reads the real source line locally for the finding snippet, because Semgrep redacts the matched line to "requires login" for unauthenticated registry rules.
verbatim: because Semgrep redacts the matched line to "requires login" for unauthenticated registry rules

subject: sca backend preference order
assertion: engine_sca.py prefers backends in order: osv-scanner (language-agnostic, reads lockfiles against OSV.dev) first, then pip-audit (Python), then npm audit (Node).

subject: sca findings grouped per package
assertion: SCA findings are grouped one per vulnerable package (carrying max severity, advisory count, IDs, and the recommended upgrade) rather than one row per CVE, because that is far more actionable.

subject: osv-scanner trust boundary
assertion: osv-scanner statically reads the lockfiles and queries the OSV.dev database; it never builds or runs the scanned target.

subject: pip-audit --disable-pip is the load-bearing safety flag
assertion: pip-audit is invoked with --disable-pip plus --no-deps; --no-deps alone does not stop pip-audit from performing a full pip resolve of requirements (which builds source distributions and executes attacker-controlled setup.py/PEP517 backends), so --disable-pip is what removes that resolve step and keeps the audit fully static.
verbatim: --no-deps alone does not stop pip-audit from performing a full pip resolve of the requirements, which builds source distributions and executes attacker-controlled setup.py / PEP517 backends (arbitrary code execution)

subject: pip-audit unpinned-requirements fallback prohibition
assertion: --disable-pip requires fully-pinned requirements; if a requirements file cannot be audited that way, PRAETOR reports SCA status error and never retries in a resolving mode.
verbatim: PRAETOR reports a status error for SCA and never retries in a resolving mode

subject: npm audit registry pinning
assertion: npm audit reads the lockfile and queries the advisory endpoint with the registry pinned on the command line, so a target-controlled .npmrc cannot redirect the audit request to an attacker host.

subject: SCA residual network trust
assertion: The SCA and Semgrep subprocesses make network calls to their advisory/registry databases as the tool's only outbound traffic; a target-controlled .npmrc can still influence npm via scoped-registry entries and ${ENV} auth-token expansion.
exceptions: --sca-backend osv avoids the npm/.npmrc concern entirely

subject: SCA tool-error versus vulnerabilities-found distinction
assertion: A non-zero SCA tool exit with parseable output means vulnerabilities found; a non-zero exit, or empty/unparseable output, without parseable results is a tool error surfaced as status error, and it is never laundered into a clean zero-findings result.
verbatim: never laundered into a clean "0 findings" result

subject: interpret.py dedup logic
assertion: interpret.py's dedup uses a category-aware key that merges the same leaked token flagged by two engines at one spot, and merges the same CWE on the same line across bundled/registry/aisec rules while recording corroboration, but keeps distinct CVEs on one package as distinct findings.
exceptions: distinct CVEs on one package stay distinct rather than merging

subject: interpret.py ranking order
assertion: interpret.py ranks findings by unified severity, then confidence, then engine, then location, and cross-engine agreement on the same issue promotes confidence to HIGH.

subject: interpret.py FP filter never deletes
assertion: interpret.py's false-positive filter heuristics move findings into a FILTERED bucket with a rationale rather than deleting them.

subject: report.py output structure and stability
assertion: report.py emits a plain-ASCII human-readable report (engine-status table, severity summary, ranked findings, the filtered bucket, and a LIMITS section) plus a stable JSON schema intended for programmatic consumers.

subject: Rust implementation is not yet runnable
assertion: A Rust workspace exists under rust/ as a second implementation, but the Python implementation is the reference implementation and the only one that can actually be run today; the Rust CLI does not wire any engine yet and exits non-zero rather than pretend to scan.
verbatim: the only one you can actually run today; The Rust CLI does not wire any engine yet and exits non-zero rather than pretend to scan.

subject: Rust port progress state
assertion: secrets is the first detector port and has a scan() entry point in rust/praetor-core/src/secrets.rs, held to the Python reference by the blocking differential runner; text.rs, sca.rs, and unicode_tables.rs remain load-bearing shared/invariant code.

subject: no Rust backend merges before its invariant test
assertion: No Rust backend may merge before its never-execute invariant test does, because every new backend widens the surface the --disable-pip guarantee must cover.
verbatim: No backend merges before its never-execute invariant test does.

subject: Rust port acceptance is differential
assertion: Acceptance of the Rust port is differential, not the tests pass: both implementations must emit identical (engine, rule_id, file, line) sets over one shared corpus, because two implementations that are not continuously reconciled are a fork, not a port.
verbatim: Acceptance is DIFFERENTIAL, not "the tests pass."

subject: differential expectation files are contracts
assertion: references/differential/*.expected files are committed contracts both implementations must reproduce and must never be regenerated to make a failing test pass, since a regenerated expectation trivially agrees with whatever produced it.
verbatim: Do not regenerate *.expected to make a test pass.

subject: a clean scan is not a safety claim
assertion: A clean PRAETOR scan means only that nothing matched these rules, never that the code is safe; every finding should be treated as a lead to verify and every clean result as an incomplete negative.
verbatim: A clean scan means "nothing matched these rules," never "this code is safe."

subject: static-analysis-only limitation
assertion: PRAETOR never runs the target, so it cannot find runtime-only bugs, logic errors, broken business-authorization, race conditions, or anything that only manifests during execution.

subject: no inter-file dataflow or taint tracking in built-in engines
assertion: The built-in engines (secrets, aisec) work line- and file-locally with no inter-file dataflow or taint tracking; Semgrep adds intra-file dataflow for its own rules, but whole-program taint analysis is out of scope for PRAETOR entirely.
exceptions: Semgrep provides intra-file dataflow for its own rules

subject: text and source files only
assertion: PRAETOR scans only allowlisted text/source files; compiled binaries, images, archives, and ordinary text-like formats outside TEXT_EXTS/TEXT_NAMES are skipped, and binary content is not seen except for base64-unwrapped content inside otherwise-text files.
exceptions: base64-wrapped content inside otherwise-text files is unwrapped and checked

subject: file size cap
assertion: Files above the size cap, default 3 MB, are skipped, so large minified bundles or data files may hide issues.

subject: secrets denylists are never exhaustive
assertion: Provider-pattern denylists are never exhaustive; new, rotated, or vendor-specific token formats not in the provider list will be missed unless the entropy detector catches them.

subject: entropy detector trades recall for precision
assertion: The generic/entropy secrets detector is tuned to avoid false-positive flooding, so it will miss low-entropy or cleverly-formatted secrets, while some high-entropy non-secrets (novel hash or ID formats) may still surface as LOW-confidence findings.

subject: secrets engine does not verify credential liveness
assertion: The secrets engine flags a secret's presence in text only; it does not verify the credential is live or that it has not already been rotated.

subject: sast coverage equals the active ruleset
assertion: SAST coverage equals the active Semgrep ruleset; a vulnerability class with no matching rule is invisible, even though the bundled rules plus default registry packs are broad.
verbatim: Coverage equals the active ruleset.

subject: sast registry packs require network on first run
assertion: Semgrep registry packs require network access on first run and results are then cached; offline mode (--no-registry) runs only the bundled baseline, giving fewer rules.
exceptions: --no-registry runs offline with only the bundled baseline

subject: some Semgrep registry rules are Pro-gated
assertion: Some Semgrep registry rules are Semgrep-Pro-gated, so unauthenticated PRAETOR runs may have reduced depth for those specific rules.

subject: SCA visibility scope
assertion: SCA sees only declared dependencies in supported lockfiles or manifests, checked against known-advisory databases (OSV, GHSA, PyPI); it cannot see vendored, dynamically-loaded, or system dependencies, and cannot find zero-days by definition.

subject: SCA advisory data freshness
assertion: Advisory data changes daily, so a clean SCA result is only as current as the database at scan time; users should re-scan regularly.

subject: SCA default severity for unrated advisories
assertion: Severity for advisories lacking both a label and a CVSS vector defaults to MEDIUM as a reasonable placeholder, not a judgment of true impact; this includes all pip-audit findings, since pip-audit's default output carries no severity.
verbatim: a reasonable placeholder, not a judgment of true impact

subject: osv-scanner recommended as safest SCA backend for untrusted code
assertion: osv-scanner, a pure static lockfile read, is recommended as the safest SCA backend to use for scanning untrusted code, in preference to the pip-audit and npm audit backends.
verbatim: Prefer osv-scanner (a pure static lockfile read) as the safest SCA backend for untrusted code.

subject: npm audit .npmrc residual risk is network-only
assertion: A target-controlled .npmrc can still influence npm audit via scoped-registry entries and ${ENV} auth-token expansion; this is a network/exfiltration consideration with no code execution, and for a hostile Node project the recommendation is to review its .npmrc first or run SCA via osv-scanner instead.
verbatim: This is a network/exfil consideration (no code execution).

subject: aisec is pattern-based and evadable
assertion: aisec is pattern-based, so a determined adversary can rephrase a prompt-injection or exfiltration payload to evade the regexes; it raises the cost of an attack and catches common and lazy cases, but does not close the class.
verbatim: it does not close the class

subject: aisec flags structure and phrasing, not intent
assertion: aisec flags structure and phrasing, not intent, so a legitimate file discussing these techniques (security docs, PRAETOR itself) can match, which is why the false-positive filter and FILTERED bucket exist and must still be reviewed rather than blindly trusted.
verbatim: It flags structure and phrasing, not intent.

subject: aisec misses novel smuggling channels
assertion: New smuggling channels, such as novel invisible code points or steganographic encodings beyond the covered set, will be missed by aisec.

subject: false positives are surfaced, never silently deleted
assertion: False positives are surfaced in a separate FILTERED bucket with a stated reason, or shown as LOW confidence, never deleted silently; the user is expected to judge them.

subject: false negatives are invisible by nature
assertion: False negatives cannot be inferred from a clean report; PRAETOR must be combined with code review, runtime testing, and defense in depth.

subject: running PRAETOR against untrusted code is safe
assertion: Running PRAETOR against untrusted code is safe, because no engine builds, runs, imports, or evaluates the target's code; the only outbound traffic is Semgrep's registry fetch and the osv/pip-audit/npm advisory lookups, and a fully air-gapped run should use --no-registry and --sca-backend osv.
verbatim: Running against untrusted code is safe
exceptions: a hostile .npmrc is a residual network/exfil consideration on the npm path, but it cannot execute code

subject: PRAETOR does not replace human security review
assertion: PRAETOR does not replace a human security review, a penetration test, or a threat model; it is a fast, repeatable first pass that catches a large fraction of common mistakes and frees a reviewer to focus on the rest.

subject: the Rust second implementation is itself a risk
assertion: A Rust workspace exists under rust/ with secrets as the first ported detector in praetor-core, but no Rust engine is wired into the CLI, so Python remains the only implementation users can run; the second implementation already exists as code even though it is not yet user-selectable.

subject: the failure mode is two implementations quietly disagreeing
assertion: A detector ported with a subtly different notion of what a line is, or which characters are letters, can produce a finding in one implementation and silence in the other while both test suites stay green; a real example was a line-definition mismatch between Python's str.splitlines() and the newline convention every other tool uses, an exploitable suppression bypass found only by porting, not by the test suite, self-scan, or code review.
verbatim: a line-definition mismatch between Python's str.splitlines() and the \n convention every other tool uses was a real, exploitable suppression bypass in this scanner, and it was found by porting

subject: differential testing's known blind spot
assertion: Differential-testing acceptance keys on (engine, rule_id, file, line) location, so it cannot detect description drift between the two implementations, and because the corpus is finite, two implementations can still share a bug on an input shape the corpus does not contain; differential testing bounds divergence but does not eliminate it.
verbatim: that comparison keys on location, so it cannot detect description drift between the two implementations, and the corpus is finite

subject: ADR-001 ruling: port to Rust
assertion: PRAETOR's engine is ported from Python to Rust incrementally, under four binding conditions; the Python implementation stays shipped and remains the reference until the Rust implementation reproduces its output exactly.
verbatim: PRAETOR's engine is ported from Python to Rust, incrementally, under four binding conditions

subject: Rust-by-default project ruling flips the burden of proof
assertion: A project-wide ruling made Rust the default language, so for any new engine or component the question is why NOT Rust here, and the answer must be explicitly named, not assumed; the ruling does not mandate rewriting already-working code.
verbatim: Default flips the burden of proof: the question is no longer why Rust here? but why NOT Rust here?, and the answer must be named, not assumed.
exceptions: does not mandate rewriting already-working code

subject: the recorded counter-argument against porting, which lost
assertion: The rejected case against porting to Rust argued the port buys nothing on the dependency story (a Rust PRAETOR still shells out to Python Semgrep and Go osv-scanner), the measured failure classes PRAETOR actually has (enumeration errors, correction-propagation failures) are not addressed by Rust, and the cost is roughly 2,900 working lines plus a long window with two implementations that could silently diverge; this objection was put to the decision-maker and overruled, Rust regardless, and is preserved so a future session can reopen it with new evidence.
verbatim: This was put to the decision-maker and the ruling was Rust regardless.

subject: original condition 1: aisec ports first
assertion: The ADR's original condition 1 ordered aisec to port first, reasoning it was pure pattern matching with zero external tool dependencies and no equivalent elsewhere, with sast/sca staying orchestration wrappers that move last.
verbatim: aisec ports first
exceptions: superseded by Amendment 2 Part B: secrets ports first, aisec is deferred

subject: condition 2: the invariant test ports first
assertion: The never-execute invariant test (tests/test_invariant_never_executes_target.py) must port before the backend it guards; no Rust backend may merge before its invariant test does, because a Rust SCA backend whose argv omits --disable-pip would reintroduce arbitrary code execution from an attacker-controlled tree.
verbatim: No Rust backend merges before its invariant test does.

subject: condition 3: acceptance is differential
assertion: Acceptance of the Rust port is differential, not the tests pass: both implementations run the same corpus and must emit identical (engine, rule_id, file, line) sets; the two-implementation window is acceptable only while that differential harness is green and blocking, and if it is ever skipped the fork becomes real that day.
verbatim: The two-implementation window is acceptable ONLY while that harness is green and blocking. If it is ever skipped, the fork becomes real that day.

subject: condition 4: SELF-SCAN-BASELINE.json is the regression floor
assertion: references/SELF-SCAN-BASELINE.json is the regression floor for both implementations and must never be regenerated to reflect an improvement, since it is the committed before state.

subject: differential corpus must include cases Python currently misses
assertion: The differential corpus must include cases the Python engine currently misses, at minimum .cursor/hooks.json-shaped agent hook configs and extensionless instruction dotfiles, otherwise identical output would be satisfied by two engines that are identically blind, certifying the existing hole into a second language.
verbatim: Otherwise "identical output" is satisfied by two engines that are identically blind, and the port certifies the existing hole into a second language.

subject: Python remains the sole runnable implementation until parity
assertion: Python remains the reference implementation until parity is reached and remains the only implementation a user can run; installation from source must keep working throughout the port.

subject: no PyPI release exists yet
assertion: Nothing is published to PyPI; the packaging metadata exists but no release has been made, so any statement about an install channel means installing from the repository.
verbatim: Nothing is published to PyPI; the packaging metadata exists but no release has been made.

subject: the JSON schema_version is the differential interface
assertion: The JSON contract's schema_version field is the interface both implementations must satisfy, and is what the differential harness compares.

subject: Windows is the native Rust build target from day one
assertion: With the verified toolchain (rustc/cargo 1.97.1, host x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, MSVC Build Tools installed), Windows is the native build target from day one, because PRAETOR is public and cross-platform and a WSL-only-developed port risks an engine that does not build for Windows users, precisely the platform where PRAETOR's Semgrep dependency already fails.
verbatim: Windows is therefore the native build target from day one

subject: cargo is not on Git Bash's PATH on this machine
assertion: cargo is not on Git Bash's PATH on this machine even though it is installed and on the Windows PATH; an earlier check wrongly concluded no toolchain from a bare cargo --version in Git Bash, so the fix is to prepend $HOME/.cargo/bin or verify with where.exe cargo before concluding a Windows Rust tool is absent.
verbatim: An earlier check concluded "no toolchain" from a bare cargo --version in Git Bash and was wrong.

subject: Amendment 1: the dependency bar for praetor-core
assertion: praetor-core's zero-dependencies property is superseded under a stated bar: a dependency is justified only when writing it ourselves would be worse for security, not merely slower to build; convenience alone is not a reason.
verbatim: The bar: a dependency is justified only when writing it ourselves would be worse for security, not merely slower to build. Convenience is not a reason.

subject: the regex crate was adopted for praetor-core
assertion: The regex crate was adopted for praetor-core because Rust's standard library has no regex, aisec and secrets are regex-driven (22 and 25 compiled patterns respectively), a hand-written matcher would be worse for security as new unaudited parsing code over attacker-controlled input, and restructuring the patterns to avoid regex would break differential parity by construction.

subject: regex crate's measured dependency footprint
assertion: Taking the regex crate pulls in 5 crates total (regex, regex-automata, regex-syntax, aho-corasick, memchr), all from the ripgrep maintainer lineage, with no build.rs anywhere in the tree, no C or system libraries, no network, and no transitive tree beyond those five; the workspace builds clean and existing tests stayed green with it present.
verbatim: No build.rs anywhere in the tree — nothing executes at build time.

subject: regex crate compatibility was checked before adoption
assertion: Rust's regex crate is a finite-automata engine that does not support backreferences or lookaround; all 47 Python patterns were swept for the lookaround and backreference syntaxes and none use any of them, so every pattern is expressible without rewriting its semantics.
verbatim: none use any of them. Every pattern is therefore truly regular and expressible without rewriting its semantics.

subject: linear-time matching benefit is noted but not yet claimed as fixing a live issue
assertion: Rust's regex engine guarantees linear-time matching versus Python's backtracking re, which matters because PRAETOR runs patterns over attacker-controlled files, but this has not been tested against PRAETOR's actual patterns, so no live ReDoS vulnerability is claimed; it is recorded only as a possible safety benefit and left open against the Python side.
verbatim: This has not been tested against PRAETOR's actual patterns, so no live ReDoS is claimed here

subject: regex dependency not yet added to Cargo.toml
assertion: The regex dependency is not yet in Cargo.toml; it was added to measure the cost analysis, then reverted, so it will land in the same change as the code that uses it rather than sitting unused in the manifest.
verbatim: The dependency is not yet in Cargo.toml.

subject: ADR-001's scope is limited to this port
assertion: ADR-001 authorizes only the Rust port of PRAETOR's engine; it says nothing about any other project's language choice and is not a license to rewrite working code elsewhere to match a Rust preference.
verbatim: It authorises the port. Nothing else.

subject: Amendment 2 Part A: the base64 crate is authorized
assertion: The base64 crate is authorized for praetor-core to port engine_secrets.py's base64 blob-inspection logic; hand-writing a decoder was judged genuinely borderline, less dangerous than a regex or JSON parser but still bespoke parsing of attacker-controlled input, and the operator's own 2026-08-22 decision was to adopt the base64 crate instead.
verbatim: Adopted, by the operator's own decision 2026-08-22.

subject: a dependency decision does not set precedent for future crates
assertion: A future crate does not inherit the base64 or regex outcome automatically; each new dependency gets its own bar-tested decision, exactly as Amendment 1 requires.
verbatim: A future crate does not inherit this outcome — it gets its own decision, exactly as Amendment 1 requires.

subject: Amendment 2 Part B: port order changes, secrets before aisec
assertion: Condition 1's original premise that aisec is pure pattern matching with zero external tool dependencies is false, because scripts/engine_aisec.py imports json and _scan_mcp structurally parses attacker-controlled MCP manifests; secrets (25 regex patterns plus base64) now fits condition 1's rationale better than aisec fits its own name, so the port order changes: secrets ports first, and aisec is deferred pending a separate JSON-parser dependency decision.
verbatim: Condition 1's stated premise is FALSE and has been for some time.

subject: aisec's JSON parser dependency decision has not been made
assertion: Porting aisec requires a JSON parser, which is a separate dependency decision that has not been made and must not be assumed to follow automatically from the base64 crate's approval, since a bespoke JSON parser over attacker-controlled input is exactly the case Amendment 1's bar exists to catch.

subject: sca.rs is argv-construction-only
assertion: rust/praetor-core/src/sca.rs exists specifically to satisfy condition 2 (the invariant test ports first) and performs argv construction only, never execution.
verbatim: argv construction only, never execution

subject: the stale condition-1 premise was found only by trying to execute it
assertion: The builder assigned the Rust port refused it twice, first because the assignment named the wrong engine against condition 1, then because condition 1's own premise did not survive contact with the code; neither was caught by review of the ADR text, only by someone trying to execute it, which is why a condition's reason must be re-derived, not just its instruction followed.
verbatim: Neither was caught by review of the ADR — both were caught by someone trying to execute it.
binds: rust/ port process; ADR maintenance discipline

subject: LF-2 is implemented and tested
assertion: LF-2, the malfunction-versus-unavailable exit-code distinction, is implemented and tested as of 2026-08-22, landed in commit 0930947, closing the hole on main; core.py defines NON_MALFUNCTION_STATUSES and engine_malfunctions, and praetor.py's report-only branch returns exit code 3 on a malfunction.
verbatim: STATUS: IMPLEMENTED AND TESTED, 2026-08-22. Landed in 0930947. The hole described below is CLOSED on main.

subject: a shipped feature requires sweeping every document asserting its old status
assertion: This document's header previously read AUTHORIZED, NOT IMPLEMENTED after the feature had actually shipped, and a session nearly assigned a builder duplicate work as a result; the lesson is that when a feature ships, every document asserting its old status must be swept, not only the one being edited.
verbatim: When a feature ships, sweep every document that asserts its old status — not only the one you happen to be editing.

subject: LF-2 authorization and its precondition
assertion: LF-2 was authorized by the operator on 2026-08-12 with the words sounds good agreed, on the precondition apply only after both adversarial audits report; that precondition was met when both passes reported the same day, recorded in references/audits/2026-08-12-independent-audit.md.
verbatim: sounds good agreed; apply only after both adversarial audits report

subject: LF-2's blast radius is a behaviour change
assertion: LF-2 is a behaviour change: report-only runs that previously exited 0 with a dead engine now exit 3.
verbatim: Behaviour change — report-only runs that today exit 0 with a dead engine would exit 3

subject: why this design lives in a committed document rather than a handoff
assertion: This design was agreed and written up, then lost at a context-compaction boundary, surviving only in a session scratchpad that dies at session close and a superseded memory file no future session had reason to open; a pre-close audit of the conversation transcript recovered it, which is why the design is committed to the repository rather than left in memory or scratch, since a commit is the only channel that survives both a memory-crossing and a session boundary.
verbatim: a commit is the only channel that survives both

subject: this document is not a general exit-code decision record
assertion: This document predates the 2026-08-13 gate work, which added a file-count floor and rejected --exclude with an empty string, so it must not be treated as a decision record for the exit-code contract generally; the table should be re-derived against current main before implementing anything from it.
verbatim: Re-derive the table below against current main before implementing; the reasoning is sound, the surrounding code has moved.

subject: LF-2's core exit-code rule distinguishes error from unavailable
assertion: LF-2's decision is that an enabled engine reporting status error yields exit code 3, never 0, in the default configuration with no --fail-on; error is deliberately distinguished from unavailable, which the prior code had treated as synonymous at exactly the boundary where they differ.
verbatim: an enabled engine reporting error yields exit 3, never 0, in the default configuration. error, not unavailable.

subject: exit-code table by engine state
assertion: Exit codes by engine state are: ok, not-applicable, or disabled yields 0 by default and 0-or-1-by-findings with --fail-on; unavailable yields 0 by default (report shows [BLIND]) and 3 with --fail-on; error yields 3 in both the default and the --fail-on cases.

subject: why unavailable is carved out of the default malfunction exit
assertion: unavailable is deliberately carved out of the default no-fail-on malfunction-exit case because a missing runtime such as Semgrep is the normal state of most Windows boxes, which is why the native/WSL/Docker fallback exists; returning 3 on every default run there would make the tool look broken and earn it a shell || true that destroys the signal, whereas a malfunction is abnormal anywhere but a missing runtime is a knowable environment fact.
verbatim: a missing runtime is a knowable environment fact
exceptions: unavailable status is excluded from the default (no --fail-on) malfunction check

subject: the carve-out is a scope decision, not a mechanism property
assertion: The unavailable carve-out is documented explicitly as the mechanism's safety scope rather than an inherent property of the mechanism, per the project's standing rule to write such carve-outs down next to the code.
verbatim: This carve-out is the mechanism's safety scope, not a property of the mechanism

subject: NON_MALFUNCTION_STATUSES is a fail-safe allowlist
assertion: NON_MALFUNCTION_STATUSES is deliberately an allowlist (ok, not_applicable, disabled, unavailable) so that an unrecognised status is treated as a malfunction by default, since the fail-safe reading of an unconsidered state is that something went wrong.
verbatim: An ALLOWLIST for the same reason GATE_TRUSTED_STATUSES is one: an unrecognised status means a state nobody here considered, and the fail-safe reading of that is "something went wrong."

subject: engine_malfunctions semantics
assertion: engine_malfunctions() returns engines that launched and broke, a failure of the run itself rather than of the scanned target; a non-empty result means the tool did not do its job, independent of whether the caller asked to gate on findings.
verbatim: Engines that LAUNCHED AND BROKE -- a failure of the run, not of the target.

subject: absence of --fail-on does not mean suppress malfunction reporting
assertion: Absence of --fail-on means do not fail me on findings, not do not tell me the tool broke; praetor . chained into a deploy must not proceed when an engine launched and died, so the default-path check is scoped specifically to malfunctions, not to every blind spot.
verbatim: No --fail-on means "do not fail me on FINDINGS". It does not mean "do not tell me the tool broke".

subject: required regression tests for LF-2
assertion: LF-2 requires five specific tests in tests/test_exit_code_never_hides_a_blind_spot.py, each with its mutation checked: an errored engine fails without --fail-on (exit 3); an unavailable runtime does not fail a report-only run (exit 0, with [BLIND] still shown); an unavailable runtime still blocks a gated run (--fail-on yields exit 3); an unknown status such as partial is a malfunction by default (exit 3); and --allow-degraded suppresses the default malfunction exit (exit 0).

subject: docs requiring simultaneous update with LF-2
assertion: praetor.py's module docstring exit-code table, README.md's exit-codes paragraph and --allow-degraded row, SKILL.md, and CHANGELOG.md must all be updated in the same commit as LF-2, and the changelog entry must state plainly and prominently, not as a footnote, that exit 3 without --fail-on is a behaviour change for any CI that runs PRAETOR report-only and tests rc != 0.
verbatim: it must be the loudest line in the entry, not a footnote

subject: PRAETOR and claude-security are complementary, not substitutes
assertion: claude-security, an LLM that reads and reasons about code, and PRAETOR, deterministic patterns plus AST/lexical context plus external static analyzers, answer different questions and neither subsumes the other: a regex cannot find a broken authorization check across four files, and an LLM cannot promise the same answer twice or run in a locked-down CI job with no model access.
verbatim: Neither subsumes the other.

subject: claude-security's own published trust-model boundary
assertion: claude-security's own SECURITY.md states that a scan and fix run under the user's Claude Code session permissions with no isolation layer of the plugin's own, so a hostile repository's .git/config, .claude/ settings, and hooks apply as usual, and the plugin does not attempt to stop a hostile repository from influencing a scan, putting anything downstream of a hostile repository explicitly out of scope.
verbatim: The code you scan is trusted. A scan and a fix run in your Claude Code session, under your permissions, with no isolation layer of the plugin's own... The plugin does not attempt to stop a hostile repository from influencing a scan.

subject: PRAETOR must run before claude-security
assertion: PRAETOR must run before claude-security on any given tree, because PRAETOR is deterministic, offline, and never executes, and it clears injection payloads, hidden Unicode, auto-run hooks, secrets, and known CVEs before an LLM reads the tree; reversing the order means the first thing to read attacker-controlled text is the component that can be talked out of its conclusion.
verbatim: Reversing them means the first thing to read attacker-controlled text is the component that can be talked out of its conclusion.
binds: recommended tool ordering for PRAETOR and claude-security users

subject: sandboxing does not stop a scan verdict from being steered
assertion: OS-level sandboxing, claude-security's recommended mitigation, bounds what a hostile repository can do to the machine, but does nothing to stop a hostile repository from steering the scan's verdict; text in a README persuading the reviewing model a file is fine is not a filesystem operation and no OS restriction sees it, and the resulting failure mode is a clean report on vulnerable code, the worst output a security tool can produce.
verbatim: the failure mode there is not damage; it is a clean report on vulnerable code, which is the worst output a security tool can produce.
binds: claude-security's sandboxing mitigation; PRAETOR's role as pre-pass

subject: recommended pre-pass command before claude-security
assertion: The recommended pre-pass before invoking claude-security is python scripts/praetor.py <target> --engines aisec,secrets --no-registry, with any PROMPT_INJECTION, DANGEROUS_HOOK, or HIDDEN_CONTENT finding triaged before proceeding to the LLM-based step.
verbatim: python scripts/praetor.py <target> --engines aisec,secrets --no-registry
binds: recommended workflow for users of both tools

subject: the pre-scan-before-LLM ordering also applies to vetting plugins and skills
assertion: The PRAETOR-before-LLM-review ordering applies to vetting plugins and skills themselves, including security-focused ones; this is in fact how the claude-security vetting analysis in this document came to exist.
verbatim: This applies to vetting plugins and skills themselves
binds: plugin and skill vetting process generally

subject: claude-security 0.10.0 vetting scan result
assertion: PRAETOR's built-in engines scanned claude-security 0.10.0, 24 text files, before adoption and found secrets 0 raw and aisec 2 raw hits; the result is stated as NO FINDING, explicitly not safe, and both aisec hits were verified by hand-reading to be false positives attributable to PRAETOR, not to claude-security.
verbatim: 24 text files. secrets 0 raw. aisec 2 raw.

subject: false positive 1: agents/explore.md prompt-injection-override
assertion: aisec matched prompt-injection-override on claude-security's agents/explore.md's own anti-injection instructions, which cite the shape of a typical override attempt so the agent can recognise and refuse it; this is the documented hazard that writing about a detector trips that detector, and even a paraphrased rewrite of the exemplar still matched, so the exemplar had to be removed entirely rather than softened.
verbatim: the exemplar had to be removed entirely, not softened. Fixed the fixture, not the rule.

subject: a praetor:ignore marker would have been the wrong fix for FP1
assertion: A praetor:ignore marker would have been the wrong fix for the agents/explore.md false positive, because the detection is correct on the text itself and what it cannot read is surrounding intent; the fact the paraphrase also fired shows this rule keys on shape alone and is a fair candidate for the lexical-context suppression aisec already supports but this rule is not benefiting from.
verbatim: A praetor:ignore marker would have been the wrong fix: the detection is correct on the text; what it cannot read is the surrounding intent.

subject: false positive 2: hooks/banner_hook.sh git-hook-network-exec
assertion: aisec matched git-hook-network-exec on hooks/banner_hook.sh's capability-probe line if python3 -c 'import sys', which is wrong on two counts: it is a plugin hook, not a git hook, and the line has no network call and no exec; the hook is display-only, fires only on UserPromptExpansion matching its own slash command, and returns no permission decision.
verbatim: Wrong on two counts: it is a plugin hook, not a git hook, and the line is a capability probe with no network call and no exec.

subject: FP2's rule name asserts evidence its predicate never required
assertion: FP2 is the more serious of the two false positives because the git-hook-network-exec rule's name asserts network/exec evidence its predicate never actually required, which the document describes as this project's own recurring failure class pointed back at itself.
verbatim: a rule whose name asserts network/exec evidence its predicate never required, which is this project's own recurring failure class pointed back at itself.

subject: both false positives were recorded, not reported to Anthropic
assertion: Both false positives are recorded as PRAETOR defects and were not reported to Anthropic, because claude-security's SECURITY.md correctly scopes PRAETOR's own scan quality out of Anthropic's vulnerability-response process.
verbatim: Both false positives are PRAETOR defects and are recorded as such, not reported to Anthropic

subject: no vulnerability was found in claude-security, so no report was filed
assertion: PRAETOR's scan is explicitly not a vulnerability report against claude-security, since no vulnerability was found, and claude-security's policy requires private responsible disclosure rather than a public issue anyway, so a look-what-we-found post would be wrong twice.
verbatim: Not a vulnerability report.

subject: the identified contribution opportunity is documentation, not a vulnerability report
assertion: The genuine potential contribution identified is documentation and integration only, running a deterministic pre-pass on untrusted code before claude-security's LLM reads it, framed as the seam where their stated out-of-scope area is PRAETOR's in-scope area; PRAETOR's own two false positives should be fixed first before offering such a contribution.
verbatim: Fix our own two false positives first.
binds: future PRAETOR and claude-security contribution work

subject: nothing has been sent to Anthropic
assertion: Nothing in this document has been sent to anyone; the document is analysis only, not outreach.
verbatim: Nothing here has been sent to anyone. This document is analysis, not outreach.
